title: Algorithms and Complexity
body:
This course answers three questions. How is an algorithm designed for a problem with no
standard answer. How is a bound on its cost proved. What happens when no efficient algorithm
exists at all.

[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] measured operations on containers that were handed to it. This
course designs the procedure itself, which means choosing a strategy before writing any code,
and proving the result is both correct and fast enough. It continues the analysis half of
that course and the theory half of [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] past the point where
either one stops.

Twelve notes across five courses already point here and state what this file owns, so the
sections below are built from those references. There are no child notes, and every link goes
out to the course or the book that covers the topic. A topic that is promised and has no note
anywhere in the vault is named in prose with no link, so nothing here claims material that
does not exist.

## Topics

### What an algorithm costs

[[Time Complexity]] covers the ladder from $O(1)$ to $O(n!)$ and how to read a bound off a
loop nest. [[Asymptotic Analysis]] covers the machinery underneath it: $O$ is an upper bound,
$\Omega$ is a lower bound, and $\Theta$ is both at once, so saying an algorithm is $O(n^2)$
leaves room for it to be faster and saying it is $\Theta(n^2)$ does not.

Complexity is a property of the algorithm and running time is a property of the machine
executing it. Constant factors are discarded because they change with the hardware and the
growth rate does not, which is why an $O(n \log n)$ sort beats an $O(n^2)$ sort on a large
input regardless of which language each is written in. The worst case is the guarantee and is
what "the complexity of X" means by default.

Both notes were written expecting this course to supply recurrence relations and the master
theorem, which cost a recursive algorithm from the shape of its own recursion. Neither has a
note in the vault. The reasoning they capture is visible directly in a divide-and-conquer
algorithm:

```
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)            split in half, solve both, combine in one pass

level 0:        n            work at this level: n
level 1:    n/2 + n/2                            n
level 2:  n/4+n/4+n/4+n/4                        n
...
depth is log₂ n levels, each doing n work   ->   O(n log n)
```

[[Proof By Induction]] in [[DISCRETE MATH]] is the technique that verifies such a bound once
there is a guess to verify.

Amortised analysis is the other loose end from second year. [[Time Complexity]] introduces it
on [[Dynamic Arrays]], where an append costs $O(n)$ on the resize and $O(1)$ every other time.
Doubling the capacity means $n$ appends trigger copies totalling $1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + n < 2n$
elements, so the whole sequence costs $O(n)$ and each append averages $O(1)$. This is a
separate question from the average case, which averages over inputs, where amortisation
averages over a sequence of operations on one structure.

### Design strategies

| Strategy | The idea | Worked in |
|---|---|---|
| Divide and conquer | split the input, solve the pieces, combine the results | [[Merge Sort]], [[Quick Sort]], [[Modified Binary Search]], [[Fast Fourier Transform]] |
| Greedy | take the locally best choice and never reconsider it | [[Minimum Spanning Tree]] with Kruskal and Prim |
| [[Dynamic Programming]] | solve each overlapping subproblem once and reuse the answer | [[Dynamic Programming]] |
| [[Backtracking]] | search every choice and prune dead branches early | [[Hamiltonian Cycle]], [[Backtracking]] |

**Greedy** is the one to be suspicious of, because it produces the wrong answer on most
problems and the failure is silent. Making 6 cents from coins of 4, 3 and 1:

```
greedy:   take 4, then 1, then 1     ->  three coins
optimal:  take 3, then 3             ->  two coins
```

The greedy choice was locally best and globally wrong, and proving a greedy algorithm correct
means proving that the locally best choice is always part of some optimal solution.
[[Minimum Spanning Tree]] is the case where that proof succeeds, and both Kruskal and Prim
work there, which is unusual enough that each carries its own argument.

**Dynamic programming and backtracking** are the same search viewed from two directions, and
both begin with [[Recursion]]. Memoising a recursion produces dynamic programming, and pruning
one produces backtracking:

```python
def fib(n):                  # O(2ⁿ): fib(30) recomputes fib(5) hundreds of times
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)

def fib(n, memo={}):         # O(n): each subproblem solved once
    if n < 2: return n
    if n not in memo:
        memo[n] = fib(n-1, memo) + fib(n-2, memo)
    return memo[n]
```

The recursion is identical in both. The only change is remembering answers already computed,
and it takes the cost from exponential to linear, which is the whole content of the technique.

**Divide and conquer** gained [[Fast Fourier Transform]] when MATH 4199 was written, and it is
the strongest entry in the table. It runs the same recurrence as [[Merge Sort]] and takes the
discrete Fourier transform from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$. At $N = 10^6$ that is $10^{12}$
operations against roughly $2 \times 10^7$, five orders of magnitude, which makes it the
clearest case in the degree of an algorithm being what enabled an application. Through the
[[Convolution Theorem]] it also reduces convolution to $O(N \log N)$, covering large-filter
image processing and multiplication of very large integers.

### Sorting, and a wall that cannot be crossed

[[Sequential Sorting]] indexes [[Bubble Sort]], [[Insertion Sort]], [[Merge Sort]],
[[Quick Sort]] and the heapsort inside [[Heap]], and it carries the argument none of them
holds individually.

Any comparison sort is a decision tree. Each comparison has two outcomes, so a tree of height
$h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, and the sort has to reach $n!$ distinct orderings to be correct
on every input. That forces $2^h \geq n!$, so $h \geq \log_2(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)$. No
comparison sort does better in the worst case, and no amount of cleverness changes it, because
the bound is about information and not about implementation. The $n!$ comes from
[[Permutation]].

Escaping that wall means giving up comparison. Counting sort, radix sort and bucket sort read
the structure of the key itself, using a digit or the value as an index, and run in $O(n)$ or
$O(nk)$ on bounded integers. No note in the vault covers them, and they are the clearest
addition this course makes to the sorting material.

### Searching

[[Search Trees]] indexes the structures by the question each one answers, and applies the same
decision-tree argument to a single query: a binary tree with $n$ outcomes has height
$\log_2 n$, so no comparison-based search does better. [[Binary Search Tree]] and
[[Balanced Tree]] hit that bound, and [[Modified Binary Search]] is the applied form on a
sorted array, where each comparison halves the remaining range.

[[Hashing]] and [[Hash Map]] get around the bound the same way radix sorting does, by
examining the bits of the key directly and comparing no whole keys at all. Tries do the same
thing on string prefixes and have no note anywhere in the vault. [[Top K Elements]] is the
practical form of the [[Heap]] argument: producing the largest $k$ items costs
$O(n \log k)$ with a heap of size $k$, against $O(n \log n)$ for sorting everything and taking
the front.

### Graph algorithms

Second year covers representation and stops, and both [[Graph]] and [[Weighted Graph]] say
that traversal belongs here. The traversal notes live in the [[Leetcode|LeetCode patterns]]
set, and the difference between the two is the whole of the topic.

| | [[Breadth First Search]] | [[Depth First Search]] |
|---|---|---|
| Frontier held in | a [[Queue]] | a [[Stack]], usually the call stack through [[Recursion]] |
| Visits | level by level outward from the source | one path to its end, then backtracks |
| Answers | fewest edges on an unweighted graph | reachability, cycle detection, connected components |

The two algorithms are the same code with one line changed, taking the next vertex from a
queue or from a stack, and that one line decides what the traversal computes.

Both operate on an unweighted graph. [[Dijkstra's Algorithm]] handles a [[Weighted Graph]] by
replacing the queue with a [[Heap]] keyed on distance so far, always expanding the closest
unvisited vertex, and its inner loop is Prim's with a different quantity in the priority
queue. The greedy choice is safe only when no weight is negative, because a negative edge
could improve a path already finalised.

[[Union Find]] makes Kruskal's question, whether two vertices are already connected, cost
effectively constant, which is why sorting the edges dominates Kruskal's running time.
[[Topological Sort]] orders a directed acyclic graph so every edge points forward, which
solves prerequisite problems and sets up dynamic programming on a DAG.

Those three live in `Leetcode/` as implementations. This course owns the reasoning behind
them: the proof that Dijkstra's greedy choice is safe under non-negative weights, why the
inverse Ackermann bound on union-find counts as constant, and what a topological order is good
for. Representation stays a cost decision, with $O(V^2)$ space for an [[Adjacency Matrix]]
against $O(V + E)$ for an [[Adjacency List]], and [[Directed Graph]], [[Vertices]] and
[[Matrix Traversal]] covering the variants.

### When no efficient algorithm exists

[[NP-Complete]] holds the definitions. P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time.
NP is the class where a proposed answer is checkable in polynomial time, which is a much
weaker requirement. A problem is NP-complete when it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces
to it, so a polynomial algorithm for one would give a polynomial algorithm for all of them.

[[Hamiltonian Cycle]] is the worked example, asking for a route visiting every vertex exactly
once and returning to the start. Finding one is NP-complete. Checking a proposed one is
$O(V)$, a single walk along the route. Its close neighbour asks for a circuit using every
*edge* once, and that has a one-line test, since such a circuit exists exactly when every
vertex has even degree. Two problems phrased almost identically land on opposite sides of
tractability, which is why the phrasing of a problem says nothing about its difficulty.

An NP-complete problem has an algorithm, and that algorithm takes exponential time.
[[Undecidability]] covers problems where no algorithm exists at any cost, which belongs to
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] and the [[Turing Machine]]. Reduction is the proof technique
on both sides of that line.

Counting is what makes the exponential concrete. [[Permutation]] and [[Combination]] in
[[DISCRETE MATH]] size a search space before anything searches it: $n!$ orderings for
[[Hamiltonian Cycle]], and $2^n$ subsets for any problem selecting a subset. At $n = 20$ that
is $2.4 \times 10^{18}$ orderings, which settles whether brute force is worth writing.

### Pattern practice

[[Leetcode|LeetCode patterns]] is the applied index over everything above, organised by
recognising the shape of the input and then selecting the technique: [[Prefix Sum]],
[[Two Pointers]], [[Sliding Window]], [[Monotonic Stack]], [[Modified Binary Search]],
[[Overlapping Intervals]], [[Fast and Slow Pointers]], [[Linked List In-place Reversal]],
[[Binary Tree Traversal]], [[Breadth First Search]], [[Depth First Search]],
[[Matrix Traversal]], [[Backtracking]], [[Dynamic Programming]] and [[Top K Elements]]. These
are interview-shaped, holding the same algorithms with the analysis removed and the
recognition drilled in its place.

## Related courses

- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) is the direct prerequisite and owns every structure
  this course runs algorithms on, including [[Tree]], [[Graph]], [[Heap]], [[Hash Map]] and
  [[Balanced Tree]]. [[Time Complexity]] and [[Asymptotic Analysis]] begin there.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613) is the other half of the theory, holding
  [[NP-Complete]], [[Turing Machine]], [[Undecidability]] and reduction as a technique.
- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271) supplies [[Proof By Induction]] for bounds on recursive
  algorithms, [[Sets]] for the definition of a [[Graph]], and [[Permutation]] and
  [[Combination]] for the size of a search space.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) is where [[Algorithm]], [[Recursion]],
  [[Data Structure]], [[Stack]], [[Queue]] and [[Linked List]] are first implemented.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] treats the same material from the self-study side in
  [[Sequential Sorting]], [[Search Trees]] and [[Minimum Spanning Tree]].
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] (COMP 3659) schedules processes, which is algorithm design under
  another name, and [[Amdahl's Law]] is a complexity argument about parallelism.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] uses gradient descent, an optimisation algorithm analysed the same
  way.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) owns [[Fast Fourier Transform]] and the
  [[Convolution Theorem]] that makes it worth running, and supplies the [[Mandelbrot Set]]
  escape-time algorithm as a worked semi-decision procedure.
- [[Leetcode|LeetCode patterns]] is the applied index over this whole course.
